name: Garlic gel

lead: Garlic gel is a home remedy rubbed onto the scalp for alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of patchy hair loss, with the aim of regrowing hair in bald spots.

Proponents say it stimulates the scalp and may calm local immune activity, though no mechanism has been established in the sources available. The only registered trial found was a small phase 3 study of a topical garlic concentrate in children that began in 2016 and was terminated after eight participants, with no results posted.

paras: It is discussed in non-prescription regrowth contexts and applied as a gel or preparation to patches of hair loss. It is used alongside or instead of standard alopecia areata treatments.
Raw garlic applied to skin has been reported to cause burns, and references advise caution, especially in young children. It is not an approved treatment for alopecia areata.

angle.text: Garlic gel is a folk remedy applied to bald patches in alopecia areata, with the hope of regrowth in those spots. One children's trial was registered and terminated after eight participants; raw garlic has caused skin burns.

lead: Garlic gel is a topical preparation made from garlic (Allium sativum) that has been used as a folk or alternative approach to hair regrowth, mainly in alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy hair loss. People apply it to bald patches hoping to see hair return, which would restore a fuller hairline and a more even scalp.

A 2007 double-blind randomized trial of 40 patients with localized alopecia areata combined topical garlic gel or placebo with betamethasone cream twice daily for three months; good or moderate responses were seen in 19 of 20 garlic-treated patients, significantly better than the placebo group, with no complications reported [1]. A 2014 evidence-based review of randomized alopecia areata trials listed garlic gel among a miscellaneous group of topical treatments with less scientific evidence [2].

A phase 3 registered trial of a topical garlic concentrate in children with alopecia areata began in January 2016, enrolled eight participants and was terminated, with no results listed [3]. A 2023 review in Cutis examined the evidence behind topical hair-loss remedies popular on TikTok, naming garlic gel along with rosemary oil, rice water and onion juice [4]. Raw garlic applied to skin has been reported to cause burns [5].

Not an approved treatment for hair loss

paras: Garlic gel and garlic extracts are applied to the scalp by some people with patchy hair loss, in the belief that garlic stimulates regrowth. The condition most associated with it is alopecia areata, in which the immune system attacks hair follicles.[2][6] Garlic gel is also named among natural remedies promoted for hair loss on social media, alongside rosemary oil, rice water and onion juice.[4]
The appearance goal is to fill in the bald patches of alopecia areata, which usually appear as a few coin-sized areas on the scalp, so the hairline and scalp look uniform again.

Alopecia areata is believed to be autoimmune: the immune system attacks hair follicles although the affected skin looks normal and unscarred. About 0.15 percent of people have it at any one time, and roughly 2 percent will have it at some point. In more than half of cases with sudden patchy onset, hair regrows within a year, and among people with only one or two patches up to 80 percent regrow hair in that period, according to Wikipedia; many people have more than one episode.[6]

Because patches often regrow without treatment, the 2014 review notes that treatment choices depend on disease duration, extent, activity and patient age, and that no universally proven therapy induces and sustains remission.[2] Established options described on Wikipedia include corticosteroid injections and creams, 5% topical minoxidil, and the JAK inhibitors baricitinib (FDA-approved June 2022), ritlecitinib (June 2023) and deuruxolitinib (July 2024).[6]

Crushed garlic produces sulfur compounds including allicin, ajoene and diallyl polysulfides; allicin is the main source of the hot sensation of raw garlic.[5] Garlic has a long history in traditional medicine in Korea, Egypt, Japan, China, Rome and Greece, and Wikipedia mentions Alexander Neckam recommending it in the 12th century for protection against the sun's heat.[5] Proponents of garlic hair remedies generally say that it stimulates or irritates the scalp and encourages regrowth; no mechanism for hair regrowth has been established in published research.

The 2014 review of 29 randomized trials in alopecia areata found no universally proven therapy and placed garlic gel in the group of miscellaneous topical and oral treatments with less scientific evidence, alongside aromatherapy, photodynamic therapy, azelaic acid, bexarotene, triiodothyronine, inosiplex and total glucosides of paeony; the reviewers judged most published trials in the field to be of moderate quality.[2] The 2007 trial is the randomized study usually cited for garlic gel.[1] A 2023 Cutis review set out to examine the evidence behind natural topical remedies promoted on TikTok, including garlic gel.[4]

Wikipedia's garlic article describes several reports of serious burns from applying garlic to the skin, including in naturopathic uses and acne treatment, some involving children; it discourages topical use of raw garlic, advises testing a small area at low concentration first and says applying raw garlic to young children is not advisable.[5] The 2007 trial reported no complications in its patients.[1]

A double-blind randomized controlled trial of 40 patients (20 per group) tested garlic gel versus placebo gel, with both groups also applying 0.1% betamethasone valerate cream twice daily, for three months in localized alopecia areata. Patch size, total hair growth and number of terminal hairs were recorded monthly; at the end, good or moderate responses were seen in 19 (95%) and one (5%) of the garlic-treated patients, significantly better than the control group (P = 0.001), and no complications were observed.[1] Because every participant also used a corticosteroid, the trial tested garlic as an add-on rather than alone.[1]

The 2014 review included garlic gel among the miscellaneous treatments assessed.[2] One phase 3 trial in children (NCT02691117) started on 10 January 2016 with eight participants and was terminated; no results are posted.[3]

Garlic gel is a home remedy discussed in natural hair-care circles and appears in 2023 coverage of hair-loss advice spread through social media, where patients implement recommendations from sources other than medical professionals.[4] It is not an approved treatment for hair loss.
